Type theory is well known to programmers (see TypeScript as an example, or the
currently very popular [TypeSafe.ai](https://docs.typesafe.ai/).
In fact, due to programming, I grew up with type theory as a basis for my 
understanding of mathematics (and by extension programming), in contrast to 
most children which are first introduced to set theory in school.

It does however intuitively make sense that these two theories are deeply
related: For example, we may have the set $\{0, 1\}$ and $\mathbb{N}$, both of
which _share_ one common Element $0$, i.e. $0 \in \{0\}$ _and_ $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
In contrast to that, we may have the type $\texttt{Bool}$ with the _terms_
$0 : \texttt{Bool}$ and $1 : \texttt{Bool}$, and the type $\texttt{Nat}$ with
the _terms_ $0 : \texttt{Nat}$, $1 : \texttt{Nat}$, $2 : \texttt{Nat}$, etc. In
this case, we have _two different terms_ $0 : \texttt{Bool}$ and $0 :
\texttt{Nat}$, which are _not equal_ to each other.

There is however a connection which goes very deep, to places most
mathematicians do not date to even go (and by extension most programmers will 
almost certainly never even heat about).
We use _Topos theory_ and its Mitchell-Benabou language to connect set theory
with type theory.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
A _topos_ is a certain kind of category (see [this previous post](todo-add-correct-link)),
which has <add missing definition concisely>.
:::

In particular, all presheaf categories are topoi, and the category of sets is a
topos, as it is the presheaf category of the terminal category 
(which has one object and one morphism).

As we now know that $\text{Set}$ is a topos, we can use the Mitchell-Benabou language to reason about
it.
<!-- By this wangSketchesElephantIntroduction source, ... -->
By [@wansingh, Definition 2.2.2], we have that given a first order theory
$\mathcal{T}$, we associate to each type $T$ of it, an object $\llbracket T
\rrbracket$ in the the model $\mathcal{C}$, a category which is a topos.
In particular, we associate to types $T$ the sets $\llbracket T \rrbracket$
under the assumption that $\mathcal{C} = \text{Set}$.
Similarily, we associate functions to function symbols ad subobjects to relation
symbols.

For more information, [@wangSketchesElephantIntroduction] is a great book about
these ideas.
